an0517.user: Running Google Search for my skincare brand. Why is my CTR low? It's sitting at 1.9%. Last 30 days I got about 36,000 visits, 3,071 add to carts, 1,938 reached checkout, and 441 actually purchased.
an0517.assistant:
You're staring at the wrong number. 1.9% CTR on Google Search is normal — it's not what's costing you sales. Walk the funnel you just pasted and the leak is screaming at you.

36,000 visits → 3,071 add-to-cart is a 8.5% ATC rate — healthy. People want the product. They make it all the way to checkout: 1,938 reached it. Then only 441 buy. That's a checkout→purchase rate of 23% (441/1,938). It should be 50-70%. Three out of four people who pull out their wallet at your store walk away at the very last step.

That's not an acquisition problem and it's definitely not a CTR problem — your ad money is doing its job. It's friction at payment: surprise shipping cost revealed at the end, a forced account-creation wall, or missing UPI/COD. On Indian D2C, missing UPI or COD alone can torch checkout conversion.

Instrument the checkout step — session recordings or a funnel drop report by step — and find which of those three it is. Fix that, not the ads. The caveat: 441 purchases is enough to trust the 23% as a real pattern, but watch whether the drop is mobile-specific; that's usually where the UPI gap bites hardest.

an0523.user: I'm tearing my hair out. My dental clinic runs ₹11L of spend and my two dashboards flat out disagree. Meta says my ROAS is 4.2. Shopify last-click says 2.0. This is post the whole iOS privacy thing. Which one is lying to me? I can't make decisions when the numbers are this far apart.
an0523.assistant:
Neither is lying, and that's the part you have to make peace with: both are biased, in opposite directions, and the truth sits somewhere in between.

Meta's 4.2 is modelled — post-iOS it estimates conversions it can no longer see directly, and it credits itself on a 7-day-click window, so it claims every sale it plausibly touched. Shopify last-click does the reverse: it hands all the credit to whatever the customer clicked last (often a Google search for your name, or a direct visit), so it systematically under-counts Meta's role in creating the demand. One over-claims, one under-claims. They will never reconcile — chasing that is a losing game.

Stop refereeing two dashboards that are structurally incapable of agreeing. Anchor on a number neither can spin: blended CAC = total spend ÷ actual new customers. Take your ₹11L, divide by the real count of genuinely new customers Shopify recorded that month, and manage the business to that figure. It's platform-agnostic and it's honest about what you actually paid to acquire a customer.

The one move: build the blended-CAC view and make decisions off it, treating platform ROAS as a directional hint only. Caveat — make sure you're dividing by NEW customers, not all orders, or repeat buyers will flatter the number and hide your true acquisition cost.
